strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: using fine-tuned and multi-agent LLMs to support High-Level Synthesis code generation, domain-specific debugging, and directive-based optimization.

The proposed ChatHLS system is reasonably comprehensive, combining HLS-C generation, verification feedback, BugRAG, hierarchical repair, DPO-based preference learning, and QoR-driven optimization in one workflow.

The authors construct a substantial domain-specific dataset, including 12,352 buggy-code examples, 3,489 preference pairs, and 4,804 optimization samples, and provide a useful taxonomy of HLS-specific errors.

Evaluation goes beyond text-only LLM assessment by measuring repair pass rates and synthesizing optimized designs with Vitis HLS on a Xilinx ZCU106 target, including latency and hardware-resource metrics.

Results are promising: HLSFixer outperforms several general-purpose LLMs on HLS error repair, and HLSTuner shows substantial latency improvements over Vitis auto-optimization, general LLMs, RAG, and several DSL-based approaches.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet adequate. The paper does not state whether code, models, BugRAG, prompts, parsers, or the constructed datasets will be released. It also omits important details such as LoRA hyperparameters, sampling parameters, seeds, candidate counts, termination conditions, exact train/test splits, and token or synthesis costs.

The central repair metric is under-specified. A successful case is not clearly defined in terms of C simulation, RTL co-simulation, functional equivalence to the golden design, timing closure, or merely eliminating a compiler/synthesis error. Without stronger correctness checks, the model could learn to suppress error messages rather than preserve program semantics.

Baseline fairness is unclear. HLSFixer benefits from domain fine-tuning, retrieval, structured error logs, multiple repair attempts, and a multi-LLM scoring panel, but it is not evident that GPT-4o, Claude, Llama, and DeepSeek receive the same tool feedback, context, prompting, or number of iterations. Model versions and decoding settings are also missing.

The external validity of VODA is limited because many training errors are produced through LLM-based bug insertion rather than collected from natural developer workflows. The paper needs stronger evidence that synthetic errors match real HLS failure distributions, along with quality-control and leakage analyses. The reported counts of 25, 34, and 24 error types should also be reconciled.

Statistical rigor is lacking. There are no confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or variance estimates for either LLM sampling or hardware synthesis, despite both being stochastic or sensitive to implementation details.

HLSTuner is evaluated on only five small, regular linear-algebra PolyBench kernels. These benchmarks are particularly amenable to pipelining, unrolling, and array partitioning. Evaluation on larger, irregular, or real-world designs and additional HLS tools/vendors is needed to support broad generalization claims.

Hardware evaluation is incomplete. The paper reports latency and some DSP/FF/LUT utilization, but omits BRAM/URAM, clock frequency, timing closure, and physical power measurements. The proposed energy-efficiency proxy is ad hoc and is not validated against measured board-level or tool-reported energy.

The headline 3.6x speedup over SOTA is difficult to reconcile with Figures 9 and 10, where the geometric-mean advantage depends strongly on the selected baseline. Comparisons with DSL methods are also not fully apples-to-apples because those methods use different source languages and annotation styles; stronger direct HLS design-space baselines would improve confidence.

Several system-design details are missing, including how agents are routed, how unknown error types are detected, how the scoring LLM evaluates candidate repairs, how many synthesis iterations HLSTuner performs, and how optimization changes are guaranteed not to alter program behavior.

The contribution is primarily domain-specific systems integration rather than a new NLP or language-learning method. This makes it a plausible applied Findings paper, but its broader significance for a main ACL audience is less clear without more general insights into LLM agents, code repair, or tool-augmented reasoning.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: high-level synthesis requires rare hardware expertise, and LLM-based debugging and directive optimization could substantially reduce developer effort.

The proposed ChatHLS workflow is conceptually coherent, combining HLS-C generation, verification-feedback-driven repair, retrieval of domain-specific error knowledge, SFT/DPO training, and QoR-based optimization. Figures 3–5 make the intended system relatively easy to understand.

The authors construct substantial domain-specific training resources, including 12,352 buggy-code samples, 34 error augmentations, 3,489 preference pairs, and 4,804 optimization samples, together with a structured HLS error taxonomy.

The repair evaluation uses 612 cases from kernel, Vitis-example, and manually constructed sources, and HLSFixer shows large apparent gains over generic Llama-3, GPT-4o, Claude, and DeepSeek models. The reported ablation also provides some evidence that explicit analysis and DPO help.
The optimization experiments use real HLS synthesis feedback from Vitis HLS and a concrete FPGA target rather than relying solely on text-generated suggestions.
weaknesses: The central end-to-end claim is not directly evaluated. The initial HLS-C generator, RAG component, agent-selection mechanism, and integrated generate–debug–optimize pipeline are not tested as one system on unseen C/C++ inputs. The reported evidence is component-level and does not establish the title's broader systematic-automation claim.

The repair metric is under-specified. A successful case is not clearly defined in terms of C simulation, RTL synthesis, timing closure, testbench coverage, or functional equivalence. No per-error-type sample counts, repeated runs, decoding variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are provided.

Dataset validity and leakage risks are not adequately addressed. Many bugs are LLM-generated through synthetic insertion, but their realism and distribution relative to developer errors are not validated. The exact train/validation/test design lists, overlap policy, and contamination controls are missing.

Baseline comparability is weak. Fine-tuned HLSFixer is compared mainly with off-the-shelf LLMs, while prior HLS-specific or hardware-oriented LLM systems cited in related work are not empirically compared. Prompting budgets, API versions, prompts, and whether baselines receive the same tool feedback are unclear.

The optimization evaluation is too narrow for the generality claimed. It uses only five small, structurally similar linear-algebra PolyBench kernels and primarily three directive families: pipeline, unroll, and array partition. Control-intensive, irregular, and larger designs are absent.

The headline speedup claims are difficult to reconcile because different figures use unclear normalizations and report 1.9×–14.8×, 3.6×, 5.4×, and 16.7× without a single explicit baseline definition. Resource utilization, timing closure, functional correctness after optimization, iteration counts, and LLM runtime/token costs are not fully reported.

The proposed energy-efficiency measure is an unvalidated proxy with arbitrary exponential and power-law terms. It should not be presented as hardware energy efficiency without comparison to measured power or an established FPGA energy model.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The paper does not report code, data, model release plans, full prompts, LoRA rank and target modules, DPO hyperparameters, seeds, baseline reimplementation details, or the complete error taxonomy.

The ablation study does not isolate the main architectural contributions such as VODA, BugRAG, multi-agent scoring, or the iterative tuning loop. The DPO gain is also small, and the underlying techniques are mostly standard combinations of RAG, SFT, DPO, and multi-agent prompting.

The work is primarily an EDA systems integration rather than a new NLP method, and several claims about rigor, reliability, few-shot learning, and broad design-quality improvements are stronger than the evidence supports. Undefined error abbreviations in Figures 6 and minor writing errors also reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent end-to-end system combining HLS-C generation, pragma optimization, tool-based verification, and iterative error repair in a multi-agent workflow.

The VODA/BugRAG data-construction pipeline is substantial, producing 12,352 fine-tuning examples and 3,489 preference pairs, with evaluation on 612 cases from kernel, Vitis-derived, and manually crafted sources.
HLSFixer shows strong empirical gains over general-purpose LLMs on HLS-specific repair, including an 82.7% average pass rate and an ablation isolating the analysis agent and DPO components.
HLSTuner is evaluated against Vitis auto-optimization, general LLMs, retrieval-augmented optimization, and several DSL/DSE methods, while also reporting resource-utilization constraints.

The architecture and workflow figures are clear, and the paper provides useful training details such as the Llama3-8B backbone, LoRA adaptation, GPU setup, optimizer, precision, epochs, and learning rates.
The work addresses a practically important problem at the intersection of code LLMs, software–hardware co-design, and automated program repair.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is primarily the integration of existing techniques—RAG, chain-of-thought, LoRA fine-tuning, DPO, and multi-agent orchestration—rather than a new NLP or learning method; the contribution may be better suited to Findings than to a main NLP conference.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper does not state whether code, models, prompts, BugRAG, or the constructed datasets will be released, and it lacks LLM versions, temperatures, seeds, stopping criteria, and detailed train/test splitting rules.

The baseline comparison may favor HLSFixer because general LLMs appear to be used in zero- or few-shot settings while the proposed system is domain-fine-tuned; prompt details, repair budgets, and statistical significance or variance across runs are not reported.

The exact definition of Pass Rate is insufficiently clear. It is not fully explained whether success requires only synthesis success, C simulation, functional equivalence to golden outputs, or all three, and testbench coverage is not analyzed.

HLSTuner is evaluated on only five PolyBench linear-algebra kernels and mainly three directive families. Timing frequency, BRAM usage, power, and other real hardware effects are not consistently considered, so cycle speedup is not necessarily end-to-end latency speedup.
The proposed energy-efficiency formula is an ad hoc proxy without validation against vendor power or energy measurements, making the Figure 11 claims less compelling.

The speedup reporting is sometimes confusing: the abstract, Figure 9, Figure 10, and conclusion use different normalizations and baselines, and the relationship among 3.6×, 5.4× geometric-mean speedup, and 16.7× is not clearly reconciled.

Ablations cover only parts of HLSFixer; there is no comparable ablation of the multi-agent architecture, BugRAG retrieval, VODA construction, or HLSTuner components, and no user study or runtime/cost analysis supports the claimed acceleration of developer cycles.

strengths: The paper presents an integrated end-to-end system for HLS-C generation, tool-feedback-driven debugging, and QoR-aware directive optimization, addressing a practical and difficult hardware-design bottleneck.
HLSFixer is grounded in actual HLS compiler, simulation, and synthesis feedback rather than only textual plausibility, and its hierarchical analysis/judge workflow is well motivated.
Evaluation is relatively comprehensive: it uses CSIM, CSYN, and COSIM verification; 108 generation tasks; 591 debugging cases; multiple benchmark suites; and MobileNet/Transformer accelerators.

HLSTuner explicitly reasons about latency and DSP/FF/LUT utilization, and the post-implementation results in Table 4 provide some evidence that the reported cycle improvements are physically realizable rather than merely simulation artifacts.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including model choice, training hyperparameters, prompts, directive configurations, benchmark sources, and a train-test similarity analysis.
weaknesses: The title and abstract overclaim generality: the evaluated system supports only PIPELINE, UNROLL, and ARRAY_PARTITION, omits DATAFLOW and AXI/interface directives, and is validated only on Xilinx Vitis and one ZCU106 platform.

The strongest baselines are general-purpose LLMs used largely zero-shot, whereas ChatHLS benefits from thousands of task-specific fine-tuning and preference examples. There is no strong baseline fine-tuned on the same data, and some C2HLSC/HLSRewriter numbers are taken from reported results with different evaluation settings.

VODA is a central claimed contribution, but the paper does not directly ablate adaptive error-case expansion against a static error repository or show that self-evolution improves performance over time. Most debugging tests also use synthetically injected bugs rather than naturally occurring developer errors.

The claim of improved "error analysis accuracy" is not supported by a separate diagnosis-accuracy metric; the reported quantity is essentially code-repair pass rate. The paper should also clearly distinguish percentage-point gains from relative percentage improvements.

Statistical rigor is limited: main bar charts lack confidence intervals, significance tests, and explicit variance across stochastic LLM runs, despite the high sensitivity of agent systems to prompts and sampling.

The leakage analysis relies mainly on Rouge-L/LCS similarity, which is weak for code and may not detect templated clones or kernel-family overlap. A design-level split and stronger code-similarity analysis are needed.
Reproducibility would be improved by an explicit release plan or URL for code, BugRAG, generated datasets, parsers, and agent configurations; the teacher data also depend on proprietary API models.

The computational-linguistics contribution is primarily application and system engineering using established SFT, DPO, RAG, and multi-agent techniques, with limited broader insight for NLP; the natural primary audience is EDA/HLS rather than ACL.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and difficult problem: making LLMs reliably generate, debug, and optimize synthesizable HLS-C rather than merely producing plausible C/C++ code.

The system is end-to-end and combines several grounded components: retrieval of Vitis documentation, specialized HLSFixer and HLSTuner agents, compiler/synthesis feedback, QoR-aware reasoning, DPO, and the BugRAG/VODA error repository.

Evaluation is stronger than a text-only LLM study because success is checked through the actual HLS tool flow, including CSIM, CSYN, and COSIM, with optimization results measured by cycles and DSP/FF/LUT utilization on a Xilinx ZCU106 target.

The evaluation includes a reasonably large number of cases—108 generation tasks, 591 debugging cases, multiple standard HLS kernels, and MobileNet/Transformer accelerators—and reports some post-place-and-route frequency and power checks.
The appendices provide useful implementation detail, including prompts, training hyperparameters, supported directives, error categories, RAG controls, token costs, and model-scale analysis.
Ablations suggest that the specialized analysis agent, DPO, and multifaceted verification process improve debugging over a single generic fixing agent.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are not fully matched. ChatHLS is a domain-fine-tuned, tool-integrated, multi-agent system trained on thousands of HLS examples, while several key baselines are frozen off-the-shelf LLMs without the same iterative QoR feedback or supervised HLS data. A same-backbone SFT baseline and a simple random/feedback-driven search baseline under equal optimization budgets are missing.

The train-test contamination analysis is methodologically flawed. Rouge-L is computed against the entire concatenated training set, whose large denominator mechanically forces small scores; this does not substitute for nearest-neighbor similarity or a documented split by base program. The overlap between canonical training and benchmark kernels remains a serious generalization concern.

Some claims are overstated or mislabeled. The reported 32.6% gain is a synthesis/verification pass-rate improvement, not a directly measured 'error analysis accuracy.' The paper also does not clearly distinguish relative gains from absolute percentage-point gains.

The causality of individual components is not fully established. In particular, VODA/self-evolving error expansion, BugRAG retrieval, the LLM-as-judge stage, and QoR-aware CoT are not sufficiently isolated from the benefits of iterative compiler feedback and heuristic resource control.

The optimization evaluation has limited external validity: it uses one Vitis version and one FPGA, supports only PIPELINE, UNROLL, and ARRAY_PARTITION, and excludes important HLS constructs such as DATAFLOW and AXI interfaces. The large geometric-mean speedups are also not uniformly reflected in the MobileNet and Transformer results.

Debugging is evaluated mainly on automatically injected, templated bugs derived from a small number of base designs. Although BugRAG draws on forum cases, the test set does not appear to contain independent real-world developer failures, so success may overstate performance in practice.

Statistical reporting is weak: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple fine-tuning seeds, or clear sampling temperatures for all pass@k experiments. API-based baselines may also change over time.

Reproducibility would be improved by an explicit release of code, data-generation scripts, checkpoints, prompts, and the exact train/test program split. The current appendices are detailed, but proprietary API baselines and dependence on a particular Vitis installation still make independent reproduction difficult.

The technical contribution is primarily an integration of existing NLP techniques—RAG, SFT, DPO, CoT prompting, multi-agent orchestration, and synthetic bug injection—for an EDA application. It is useful engineering, but the methodological novelty for computational linguistics is limited and the paper may fit an EDA/embedded-systems venue more naturally.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and difficult problem: LLM-generated HLS-C often violates synthesizability constraints, while directive tuning has a large, non-linear design space. The generation, debugging, and QoR-aware optimization components map clearly to the stated bottlenecks.

Evaluation is unusually tool-grounded for an LLM-application paper: success requires passing C simulation, synthesis, and C/RTL co-simulation, and optimized designs are additionally checked after place-and-route. This is substantially more reliable than text-similarity or LLM-judge evaluation.

The authors construct sizable domain datasets—10,878 debugging samples covering 33 error types and 4,804 optimization samples—and provide training hyperparameters, prompt examples, error taxonomies, and a Rouge-L analysis intended to reduce train-test overlap.

The empirical comparison is broad, including general-purpose LLMs, matched RAG baselines, prior HLS-C generation systems, Vitis auto-optimization, DSL-based approaches, and a learning-based DSE method. Ablations, per-error results, model-scale analysis, token costs, and optimization trajectories add useful insight.

The reported results suggest practical value under explicit resource constraints, including speedups on standard HLS kernels and MobileNet/Transformer accelerators, while the authors explicitly acknowledge limitations in supported directives and hardware platforms.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is primarily an integration of existing techniques—multi-agent prompting, RAG, SFT/DPO, tool feedback, and NSGA-II-generated training data—rather than a new NLP or learning method. Its relevance to a broad ACL audience is therefore somewhat specialized and EDA-centered.

Several algorithmic details needed for full reproducibility are missing. There is no pseudocode for HLSTuner's iterative proposal/selection/backtracking policy, its action space, termination criteria, feedback parsing, or failure recovery. VODA's deduplication, error-quality control, and expert-verification process are also underspecified, and no code or artifact release is explicitly promised.

The debugging benchmark is mainly synthetic: 591 cases are generated by automated bug injection from 35 base designs rather than collected from real developer failures. The generation benchmark has only 108 tasks, optimization is evaluated on a modest kernel set, and all hardware validation uses Vitis and one Xilinx platform. Generalization to real codebases, other HLS compilers, FPGAs, and directives such as DATAFLOW or AXI remains uncertain.

Statistical rigor is limited. LLM outputs are stochastic, but the paper provides no confidence intervals, significance tests, bootstrap estimates, or error bars for pass rates or speedups. The geometric speedups are accompanied by large per-kernel variance, so it is difficult to assess stability or the influence of outliers.

The pass@k protocol should be stated more precisely, including temperatures, sample counts for each reported number, and whether the values are empirical pass rates or unbiased pass@k estimators. The denominators and exact comparators behind headline improvements such as 32.6%, 41.8%, and 3.3× should also be consolidated in one table.

The causal evidence for key design choices is uneven. Although HLSFixer has useful ablations, HLSTuner lacks ablations that isolate QoR-aware chain-of-thought, iterative synthesis feedback, and the NSGA-II-constructed optimization data. Similarly, successful repair does not directly measure error-diagnosis accuracy, so claims about error-analysis accuracy are not independently validated.

Baseline fairness needs more discussion. General LLMs, RALAD using a different proprietary model, DSL-based systems, Vitis defaults, and HGBO-DSE have different input languages, action spaces, tool access, and search budgets. The evaluation should make prompts, retrieved context, iteration limits, synthesis budgets, and wall-clock costs as comparable as possible.

Some terminology is stronger than the evidence supports. VODA is described as self-evolving, but the experiments do not demonstrate continuous adaptation after deployment; the QoR-aware model learns qualitative trends rather than precise hardware prediction; and the place-and-route validation is reported only through aggregate min/mean/max statistics rather than full per-design results.
